summary: For ages 13–14 (KS3→KS4 boundary), learners build the motor effect: a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force that is perpendicular to BOTH the current and the field, and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force. The lead activity is a predict → observe → reconcile cycle on a motor-effect bench (physical demo or live simulation) with independent reverse-current and reverse-field controls, so each cause is isolated and the direction pattern (later named the left-hand rule) is discovered rather than handed down. Complementary activities attack the non-intuitive 3D perpendicularity, drill direction prediction, and label motor/loudspeaker parts. At KS3 the goal is to predict and observe the motion and connect it to the motor and loudspeaker; the quantitative F = BIL and a full field-interaction explanation belong to KS4 and later.
misconceptions: Importing 'opposites attract' from electrostatics to current-carrying wires (Singh).
Expecting the wire to be pushed TOWARD a pole (along the field) rather than perpendicular to it (Singh).
Believing the force and the field point in the SAME direction — a gut-feeling error, strongest when shown real apparatus (Singh).
Mixing up the 'field from a current' rule and the 'force on a current' rule (Singh).
Treating the multi-step reasoning (field, then force) as a single guess, and memorising outcomes (e.g. 'opposite currents repel') without being able to reason them (Singh).
Thinking the explanation of HOW the two fields interact is required at this level — it is deliberately out of scope (Oak/IOP).

activities.title: Motor-effect bench: predict, run, reconcile
steps: View a straight wire hanging between a north and a south pole, seen end-on (use real slab/Magnadur magnets on an iron yoke with a stiff copper wire or foil strip, or a live end-on simulation).
BEFORE switching on, predict which way the wire will move and say why.

Run it and observe: from rest the wire kicks SIDEWAYS, perpendicular to both the current and the field — either out of the gap or deeper into it, depending on the current and field directions — not toward either pole.
Use an independent reverse-current control: flip only the current and observe the kick reverse.
Use an independent reverse-field control: flip only the magnets and observe the kick reverse again.
Flip BOTH current and field together and predict first — observe that the kick returns to the original direction.
After several (current, field) → force rounds, state the pattern you found in your own words; then meet the left-hand rule as a summary of that pattern.

'Roll the wire up' into a coil and observe that, because the current flows in opposite directions along the two sides, they feel forces in opposite directions, which together turn the coil (a motor; a split ring reverses the current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way); see how a changing current drives a cone in a loudspeaker.
activities.insight: The force on a current-carrying wire is perpendicular to both the current and the field; reversing either input reverses the force while reversing both restores it; a wire that is free and initially at rest therefore starts to move in the direction of that force, and the same force turns a motor coil and moves a loudspeaker cone.

activities.title: Orienting the three axes: force ⊥ both current and field
steps: Work with three mutually-perpendicular axes representing current, field (N→S), and force — using a physical three-axis hand/prop, or a 3D model you can reorient and view from any angle.
Set the current axis and the field axis in space, then identify the force on the third, perpendicular axis.
Rotate the viewpoint to confirm the force stays perpendicular to both regardless of how you look at it.
Explore the special cases: the force is maximum when the wire is perpendicular to the field, and zero when the wire lies along the field.
activities.insight: The force is always perpendicular to both the current and the field; when the wire is at right angles to the field (where the force is largest), current, field and force are all mutually perpendicular — a genuinely three-dimensional relationship that a single flattened view can hide.

activities.title: Predict the force direction and separate the two rules
steps: Given a current direction and a field direction, predict which way the force pushes the wire.
Answer reverse-current and reverse-field tasks: state how the force direction changes when only one input flips, and when both flip.
Sequence the reasoning: first identify the field, THEN apply the force rule — do not treat it as a single guess.
Match a motor and a loudspeaker to the motor-effect principle they rely on.
Distinguish 'the field produced by a current' from 'the force on a current in a field' when a question could invite either.
activities.insight: Direction of the force follows reliably from the current and field via multi-step reasoning, and the 'field from a current' rule is not the same as the 'force on a current' rule.

activities.title: Label the arrows, the motor and the loudspeaker
steps: Label the three arrows on a wire-between-poles diagram: current, field (N→S), and force.
Label the parts of a D.C. motor (coil, magnets, split ring) and a loudspeaker (coil, magnet, cone).
Use a left-hand-rule reference card to check the arrow directions.
Explain in a sentence how the force on the coil's two sides produces rotation, and how a changing current moves the cone in and out.
activities.insight: The same perpendicular force appears in a diagram, a motor and a loudspeaker; the parts and arrow directions can be named and connected to the principle.

checkQuestion: A wire carrying a current sits between the poles of a magnet, and the wire suddenly jumps — it feels a force. Which way does the force push the wire, compared with the current and the magnetic field — and what happens to that push if I reverse ONLY the current?
checkAnswer: The force is at right angles to BOTH the current and the field (not along either) — it pushes the wire perpendicular to the field lines and to the current direction. Reversing only the current reverses the direction of the force, so the wire jumps the other way. (Reversing the field alone also reverses it; reversing both leaves it unchanged.)
